video_title: This Is How New York City Takes Out Its Trash | Odd Lots
gist: Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal interview NYC Sanitation Deputy Commissioner Joshua Goodman on how the city handles 24 million pounds of waste a day and its 'trash revolution': a data-driven move from curbside black bags to building-assigned on-street containers, with a custom side-loader truck and full rollout funded by end-2031. The episode also covers waste export by barge and rail, NYC's contract-protected recycling, compost and biogas, and the idea of designing streets so that every space belongs to someone.

themes.theme: Scale and economics of NYC's waste system

insights.claim: The NYC Department of Sanitation picks up, processes and exports 24 million pounds of trash, recycling and compostable material every day for about 8.5 million residents.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of a recurring, non-discretionary municipal logistics market (trucks, containers, rail/barge export, processing).

insights.claim: Residential trash collection in NYC is a free, unlimited, non-means-tested service, while businesses must pay private carters, and the department intends to preserve universal service through any modernization.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: No pay-as-you-throw pricing means heavy wasters are effectively subsidized; any shift to pricing would be a major political choice.
insights.quote: You put it out, we come and get it.

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal argues there is an underlying political choice in not making residential garbage pay-as-you-go, raising the question of whether heavy wasters are subsidized by light wasters.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Pay-per-pound pricing is a latent policy lever that would change waste volumes and municipal revenue.

insights.claim: After the Staten Island landfill closed around 2000, the city spent a multibillion-dollar, 15-year program building five transfer stations that containerize waste for export by barge or rail instead of trucks.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Waste export via barge and rail creates long-term demand for rail/barge haulage and out-of-city disposal capacity.
insights.quote: was a multibillion dollar, 15-year infrastructure project to build five transfer stations around the city

insights.claim: Collection trucks hold about 12-13 tons each, run mostly between midnight and 8:30am, and routes are optimized so trucks fill up and finish within a single shift.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Route density and payload drive unit economics of collection, relevant to fleet and route-optimization vendors.

insights.claim: NYC actually produces less trash per person than most other Western cities, contradicting the common claim that its volume makes containerization impossible.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Undercuts the exceptionalism argument against adopting global best-practice waste infrastructure.

insights.claim: NYC's recycling is protected by long-term contracts guaranteeing beneficial reuse, so properly sorted cans and bottles become new products, which Goodman says rebuts the 'recycling is a scam' claim at least for NYC.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Long-term offtake contracts insulate municipal recycling from commodity-price collapses; a template for de-risking recycling.

insights.claim: Recycling is market-based: many materials like styrofoam are chemically recyclable but too light for any manufacturer to aggregate profitably, so what is accepted depends on economics rather than chemistry.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Recyclability is an economic, not technical, question; material density and aggregation drive whether streams have value.
insights.quote: It's a good, example of how this is actually a market based system for recycling

insights.claim: Long-term planning shielded NYC from China's 2017-2018 import policy changes that collapsed many cities' recycling markets, and NYC avoided single-stream mixing of paper with metal/glass/plastic, which proved a money loser for cities that adopted it.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Single-stream recycling carries contamination and margin risk; sorting technology is not yet good enough per the department.

insights.claim: NYC's metal, glass and plastic go to a Sunset Park facility for sale into recycling markets, while paper goes to a Staten Island mill where pizza boxes are a primary product.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Closed-loop paper recycling feeding local packaging production shows a near-immediate domestic market for recovered fiber.
insights.quote: Cardboard and paper that you recycle today might become a new pizza box tomorrow.

insights.claim: Compost is the newest and biggest growth stream: food waste goes mainly to a 33-acre Staten Island facility, with about 15 million pounds of finished compost given away this summer, and some goes to Newtown Creek digesters producing biosolids and biogas that heats Brooklyn homes.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Organics diversion expands demand for anaerobic digestion and renewable natural gas infrastructure.

insights.claim: No North American city does on-street containerization; when NYC's program is implemented it will go from the back of the pack to first in North America.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: NYC becomes a reference customer and template for other North American cities' container and truck procurement.

insights.claim: Because weight had been the century-old efficiency metric, DSNY conducted a 70,000-block volumetric analysis converting weights to volumes, sizing containers for one extra day of capacity and mapping curb cuts, hydrants and tree canopy.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Shows the data groundwork required before municipal containerization procurement can scale.
insights.quote: we had to do a 70,000 block volumetric analysis

insights.claim: NYC rejected Europe's open shared-bin model, partly because free open bins would let businesses (which pay private carters) dump into residential capacity, and instead assigns bins by building size: wheeled bins for 1-9 units, on-street 'Empire bins' for 31+ units, and a choice for 10-30.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Building-assigned bins avoid free-riding and turf disputes, a design choice affecting container volumes and specs.

insights.claim: Containerization launched in Manhattan Community District 9 (West Harlem) in June 2025, expands to Brooklyn Community District 2 in fall 2026, and the mayor committed to funding full rollout across 59 districts by end-2031, with the remaining 57 in about five years.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Defines a multi-year procurement ramp for bins, side-loader trucks and related services through 2031.
insights.quote: the mayor has actually committed to funding this program for a full rollout by the end of 2031

insights.claim: Lacking a suitable automated side-loader truck for NYC residential streets and facing a roughly five-year design timeline, DSNY built a prototype in about ten months combining a European side-loading body, a Mac chassis (as transcribed) and an electronics integrator; about 20 are operating out of a ~2,300-truck fleet.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Signals a multi-year fleet replacement opportunity for truck chassis, body and integration vendors as rollout scales.
insights.quote: we got a prototype truck built in about ten months

insights.claim: The 2022 Future of Trash report estimated containerization could take up to 150,000 of NYC's roughly 3 million parking spaces, but detailed implementation analysis cut that to about 30,000 at full rollout, possibly fewer with opt-ins.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Curb-space cost is about a fifth of initial fears, lowering political resistance to rollout.
insights.quote: it was more like 30,000 spaces at full rollout

insights.claim: Barcelona, often called the gold standard, told NYC it over-converted its fleet to side loaders and had to reacquire rear loaders for loose bags and bulky items, so NYC is keeping rear loaders for bulky waste.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Fleet mix will remain hybrid, sustaining demand for rear-loader trucks alongside side loaders.

insights.claim: About 50% of sanitation workers' line-of-duty injuries are sprains and strains from throwing bags, so mechanized side-loading collection should materially reduce injuries; crews stay at two per truck.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Automation lowers workers' comp and injury costs without headcount cuts, easing labor acceptance.

insights.claim: DSNY has about 6,500 sanitation workers out of 10,000 total staff, and needle-stick injuries have risen sharply, which the department attributes to increased GLP-1 use with online-pharmacy purchasers discarding needles in trash.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: An unexpected second-order effect of GLP-1 adoption: growing sharps disposal and worker-safety costs in municipal waste.
insights.quote: we assume it's from an increase in GLP one usage

themes.theme: Design over messaging: the politics of cleanliness

insights.claim: Black bags became NYC's norm because the 1811 street grid left no alleys and, after the 1968 sanitation strike, a Mayor Lindsay task force adopted plastic bags pushed by the plastics industry as rodent resistant, which they were not.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Path dependence from infrastructure and industry lobbying can lock in suboptimal municipal systems for decades.
insights.quote: the plastics industry pushed them as

insights.claim: Goodman rejects LaGuardia's 'no Democratic or Republican way to pick up garbage' as patently untrue, arguing who you prioritize (drivers vs. pedestrians) is ideological.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Municipal service design is a political allocation of public space, shaping infrastructure budgets.

insights.claim: DSNY sees the built environment as more important than anti-littering ad campaigns, applying Oscar Newman's Defensible Space idea so every part of the street belongs to someone, which is why Empire bins are assigned to specific buildings.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Ownership-based design is expected to drive cleanliness more than outreach, guiding where cities allocate spending.

insights.claim: A 2018 one-district pilot removing all litter baskets (Tokyo/Mexico City model) failed, as people littered everywhere, though Goodman wants to revisit after full containerization since piles of trash attract more trash.
insights.speaker: Joshua Goodman (Deputy Commissioner, NYC Department of Sanitation)
insights.so_what: Cleanliness models don't transfer directly; sequencing matters.

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal defends NYC's roughly $1.5 million McKinsey trash study, arguing the volumetric data collection was genuinely hard and cities shouldn't keep such expertise in-house for once-a-decade studies.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Supports a recurring role for consultants in infrequent large municipal infrastructure redesigns.
